title: UML Class Diagrams
summary: The notation interviewers expect on a whiteboard: class boxes, the four relationship arrows, and multiplicities — read and drawn fluently under time pressure.

slides.markdown:
A UML class diagram shows the classes in a system and how they relate — inheritance, containment, association — as boxes connected by lines. In interviews it's the fastest way to prove you can turn a fuzzy requirement into a concrete object model without a wall of prose.

Think of it as a blueprint: each box is one class, each line is a relationship with its own precise meaning. This topic covers the exact notation — box anatomy, the four relationship arrows, and multiplicities — so you can read and draw it fluently under interview time pressure.

slides.sectionTitle: Why interviewers want a diagram, not just prose
slides.markdown:
When you describe a design only in prose — "the Order has Payments and belongs to a Customer" — an interviewer can't tell if that's one Payment or many, or whether an Order can exist without a Customer. A quick class diagram forces you to commit: multiplicities, the direction of the relationship, and who owns whom.

It also compresses time. A five-minute sketch communicates what would take three minutes of careful, ambiguity-prone prose, leaving more of the interview for trade-offs instead of you narrating your own design back to yourself.

Drawing first, narrating second, is a stronger signal than talking through a design that was never actually pinned down on paper.

slides.sectionTitle: Class box anatomy: name, attributes, methods, visibility markers
slides.markdown:
A UML class box has three stacked compartments: **name** on top, **attributes** in the middle, **methods** at the bottom. Each attribute and method line starts with a visibility marker: `+` public, `-` private, `#` protected, `~` package-private.

A typical line reads `- balance: double` (a private attribute named balance of type double) or `+ withdraw(amount: double): boolean` (a public method taking a double, returning a boolean). Interviewers read these markers as a proxy for whether you think about encapsulation at all, not just naming.

Skip a compartment only when it's genuinely empty — an interface with no attributes, for example — never just to save time.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a fully annotated UML class box
slides.markdown:
Here's a `BankAccount` class box with every part labeled, so you can see how the compartments and visibility markers from the previous slide actually look on paper.

```
+-------------------------------+
|          BankAccount           |  <- class name (centered)
+-------------------------------+
| - accountId: String            |  <- private attribute (-)
| # balance: double              |  <- protected attribute (#)
| + owner: Customer              |  <- public attribute (+)
+-------------------------------+
| + deposit(amt: double): void   |  <- public method (+)
| + withdraw(amt: double): bool  |
| - validate(amt: double): bool  |  <- private helper method (-)
+-------------------------------+
```

On a real whiteboard you'd drop the type annotations for speed and keep just names — the compartments and visibility markers are what actually carry the model.

slides.sectionTitle: Association vs aggregation vs composition — the diamond notation and lifecycle implications
slides.markdown:
Three relationship types share a similar-looking line but mean very different things. A plain **association** (a line, no diamond) means two classes are related with no ownership implied — a `Student` and a `Course` just know about each other. **Aggregation** (open diamond `◇` at the owner) is a "has-a" relationship where the parts can outlive the whole — a `Team` has `Player`s, but a disbanded team's players go play elsewhere. **Composition** (filled diamond `◆`) is a stronger "owns-a" where the part's lifecycle is tied to the whole — an `Engine` is destroyed when its `Car` is.

The diamond always sits on the side of the *owner* — reverse it and the notation says the opposite of what you meant. The lifecycle question — "does the part survive without the whole?" — is the fastest way to pick the right one under pressure.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: aggregation vs composition drawn side by side (Car–Engine vs Team–Player)
slides.markdown:
```
Composition (filled diamond — owns, shares lifecycle):
  Car ◆──────────── Engine
  (destroy the Car, the Engine goes with it)

Aggregation (open diamond — has, independent lifecycle):
  Team ◇──────────── Player
  (disband the Team, the Players keep playing elsewhere)
```

Both diamonds sit next to the *whole* (`Car`, `Team`), never the part — that placement is what tells a reader which class owns the relationship. If you can't decide which diamond to draw, ask whether deleting the whole should cascade-delete the part: yes means composition, no means aggregation.

Two more arrows round out the relationship set. **Inheritance** — a solid line with a hollow triangle pointing at the parent — means "is-a" between two classes: `SavingsAccount` inherits from `Account`. **Realization** — a *dashed* line with the same hollow triangle — means a class implements an interface's contract without inheriting any implementation: `BankAccount` realizes `Payable`.

The distinction matters in interviews because it signals whether you're modeling shared *implementation* (inheritance, solid line) or a shared *contract* (realization, dashed line). Defaulting every relationship to solid-line inheritance because "it implements the interface" is a tell that you haven't internalized the difference — interfaces get the dashed arrow, always.

Multiplicities sit at each end of a relationship line and answer "how many?" from that class's perspective. `1` means exactly one, `0..1` means zero or one (optional), `0..*` (or just `*`) means zero or more, and `1..*` means at least one.

Read a number attached to the *far* end: in `Order "1" —— "1..*" OrderLine`, one `Order` has one-or-more `OrderLine`s, and reading from the other side, each `OrderLine` belongs to exactly one `Order`. Swapping which number sits next to which class is the single most common notation mistake — double-check before you commit ink.

Interviewers use multiplicities to probe edge cases: can an `Order` exist with zero `OrderLine`s? Your `0..*` vs `1..*` choice is the answer.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: translating a small class hierarchy into its UML diagram
Pitfall: confusing aggregation and composition when the lifecycle question is asked
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Aggregation and composition are basically the same thing, just draw whichever diamond looks right."

**Why it's wrong:** the two notations encode different lifecycle guarantees, and an interviewer who asks "what happens to the Engine if you delete the Car?" is testing whether you actually mean what you drew. Answering "nothing, it's independent" right after drawing a filled composition diamond contradicts your own diagram.

**Correct model:** decide the lifecycle answer *first* — does the part get deleted when the whole does? — then pick the diamond that matches: filled for yes (composition), open for no (aggregation). The diagram should follow your design decision, not the other way around.
